lead: Inheritance lets a new class reuse the attributes and methods of an existing class. The existing class is the base class, parent class or superclass. The new class is the derived class, child class or subclass. The child gets the parent's members and can add its own. This avoids copying the same code for every related type. Python supports single, multiple and hierarchical inheritance. The built-in super() calls the next class in the method resolution order, usually the parent, so constructors can chain. Frameworks, GUI toolkits and banking models use inheritance to share common behaviour.
prereq: You need: 4.1 classes and objects, 4.2 constructors and self, and 4.3 encapsulation.

blocks.text: Write class Student(Person):. The parentheses mean Student is a child of Person. Person is the base class; Student is the derived class. This is single inheritance: one direct parent. The child inherits name and any methods Person defines. It may add roll. The relation is an is-a relation: a Student is a Person. A Person is not necessarily a Student.

Hierarchical inheritance has one base class and many child classes. Person can be the base for Student and Teacher. Student adds roll; Teacher adds subject. Both reuse the name handling in Person. A child can also be a parent for another class, as in class Monitor(Student). That is multilevel inheritance: Person → Student → Monitor. Keep the chain short; deep chains make code hard to follow.

The child does not copy the parent code. Python looks in the child first, then in the parent. If the child defines no __init__, it uses the parent constructor. If the child defines its own __init__, the parent part is not initialised unless the child calls the parent constructor. Overriding is in 4.5.

items: isinstance(obj, Base) is True for a child object; issubclass(Child, Base) is True for the class.

blocks.text: Multiple inheritance lists more than one parent: class C(A, B). C gets attributes and methods from A and B. Python searches C, then A, then B, following the method resolution order (MRO). The MRO is the class search order for attributes; full C3 details are in 4.5. If both parents define a method with the same name, the left parent wins unless the child overrides it.
isinstance(obj, C) returns True if obj is an instance of C or any child of C. issubclass(D, C) returns True if D is C or a child of C. These checks are common in validation and framework code.

Multiple inheritance is useful for mixins: small classes that add one behaviour. It can create diamond-shaped graphs. Use it only when the is-a relation is clear for every parent. Multilevel inheritance is a chain, not a fan-in: class C(B), class B(A).

super() gives access to the next class in the MRO. In single inheritance, super().__init__(name) calls Person.__init__ from Student.__init__. This initialises self.name before Student stores self.roll. Without the call, s.name does not exist and reading it raises AttributeError.

items: In multiple inheritance, super() calls the next class in the MRO, not every parent. Cooperative classes pass arguments along the chain.

blocks.text: Use super() instead of Person.__init__(self, name) when you want the chain to work with multiple inheritance. The explicit form hard-codes one parent. super() with no arguments works inside an instance method. It uses the current class and self to find the next class. Overriding methods and the full MRO are in 4.5.
In multiple inheritance, super() does not mean 'call every parent'. It calls the next class in the MRO. Cooperative classes pass arguments along the chain so each parent part runs once.

figure.caption: Person is the base class; Student with roll 23 and Teacher with subject Python are two child classes in a hierarchical inheritance tree. Notice that both children reuse the name attribute from Person.

spec.aria: Person is the base class; Student with roll 23 and Teacher with subject Python are two child classes in a hierarchical inheritance tree.

examples.question: Write Python classes Person, Student(Person) and Teacher(Person). Person.__init__(name) stores name. Student.__init__(name, roll) calls super().__init__(name) and stores roll. Teacher.__init__(name, subject) calls super().__init__(name) and stores subject. Create s=Student('Ravi', 23) and t=Teacher('Meera', 'Python'). Print s.name, s.roll, t.name and t.subject, each on its own line. Give the exact output.
steps: Person.__init__ receives name='Ravi' for s and stores self.name='Ravi'.
Student.__init__ receives name='Ravi' and roll=23. It calls super().__init__('Ravi'), so s.name='Ravi'. Then it stores s.roll=23.
Person.__init__ receives name='Meera' for t and stores self.name='Meera'.
Teacher.__init__ receives name='Meera' and subject='Python'. It calls super().__init__('Meera'), so t.name='Meera'. Then it stores t.subject='Python'.
The four print calls produce the lines Ravi, 23, Meera and Python. The numeric roll value is 23.
examples.answer: The output has four lines: Ravi, 23, Meera and Python; the stored roll value is 23.

traps: Forgetting super().__init__(...) leaves the parent part uninitialised. Reading s.name then raises AttributeError.
In multiple inheritance, super() does not mean 'call every parent'. It calls the next class in the MRO.
class Student(Person) is inheritance; class Student: is not. A missing parent in the parentheses loses all reuse.
isinstance(s, Person) is True for a Student object, but isinstance(p, Student) is False for a plain Person object.
Multiple inheritance order matters: in class C(A, B), A is searched before B unless C overrides the name.

quiz.q: Write the syntax for a class Child that inherits from Base.
quiz.a: class Child(Base): followed by the indented class body.
It runs Person.__init__ so self.name is created. Without it, s.name is missing.

quiz.q: Given class A: pass, class B(A): pass, class C(B): pass, and c=C(), give the truth values of isinstance(c, A) and issubclass(C, A).
quiz.a: Both are True: C is a child of B, and B is a child of A.

quiz.q: In class C(A, B), both A and B define show. C does not. Which show runs when c.show() is called, and why?
quiz.a: A.show runs, because the MRO searches C then A before B; the left parent wins when the child does not override. Full C3 order is in 4.5.

quiz.q: Define hierarchical inheritance in one sentence.
quiz.a: One base class has two or more direct child classes.

quiz.q: Write only the class header and __init__ for Teacher(Person) that stores name and subject, using super().
quiz.a: class Teacher(Person): with def __init__(self, name, subject): super().__init__(name); self.subject = subject.

quiz.q: A student writes super().__init__() in a child of two parents and expects both parent constructors to run. Is that correct?
quiz.a: No. super() calls the next class in the MRO, not every parent. Each class in the chain must cooperate and call super().

beyond: Not for the exam. Python's real method resolution order is C3 linearisation, which handles diamonds without repeating a class. GUI toolkits and web frameworks use cooperative super() so mixins compose cleanly. Search 'Python C3 linearization', 'cooperative multiple inheritance' and 'isinstance abstract base class'.
